Thank you for sending your work entitled “Widespread correlation patterns of fMRI signal across visual cortex reflect eccentricity organization” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by Eve Marder (Senior editor), Timothy Behrens (Reviewing editor), and 3 reviewers.

The Reviewing editor and the reviewers discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

You can see the comments below. During our discussion, the central concerns with your manuscript are the overlap with Raemaekers et al. Neuroimage 2013 and disagreement between the two studies of the extent of the bias towards eccentricity rather than homotopic or polar connectivity.

It will be very important in your revisions to include a thorough discussion of these points. It would also be useful if there are further analyses you can try that may address these issues directly. It is of particular interest whether your data quality are adequate to disambiguate the different possibilities (see last comment R3). It was clear from the discussion among the reviewers that it is essential to address this point if eLife are to consider publishing a revision.

Reviewer #1:

This is an impressively careful and thorough study of an important set of phenomena related to resting-state functional connectivity in human visual cortex. Several previous studies cited by the authors have identified resting-state correlations that include retinotopic components and other components that are spatially more widespread. The current study systematically examines the spatial pattern of correlations using two resting-state paradigms (with eyes closed and eyes open), plus a paradigm involving watching a movie while fixating. The most significant finding is that for all 3 paradigms the spatially extended correlations are stronger along iso-eccentricity bands. There is also a weaker component related to polar angle and another component related to homotopic (mirror-image retinotopy) in the opposite hemisphere.

In the Discussion, the authors attempt to provide a neurobiologically plausible interpretation of the strong eccentricity-related functional correlations analyzed in this study. In this reviewer's opinion, the results remain intriguing but still quite puzzling. However, the careful analysis done in this study represents a major advance, and it will likely stimulate further explorations aimed at better understanding the functional significance of these phenomena.

The manuscript is well reasoned and well written, and needs only minor revisions in the opinion of this reviewer.

Minor comments:

1) Both the Abstract and Introduction refer to evidence for more than two dozen retinotopic areas in human visual cortex. However, neither of the cited articles (Silver and Kastner, 2009; Wandell and Winawer, 2011) actually document evidence for two dozen retinotopic areas. Either the statement should be toned down (it is not critical to the study) or appropriate references should be added.

2) Results section, Materials and Methods section and Figure 2.

Please state the extent of visual stimuli for the retinotopic mapping (was it 30 degrees along the meridia, as in Arcaro et al., 2011?). Also, add a scale bar for the eccentricity maps in Figure 2B. Finally, consider clarifying that 'peripheral' really means 'near periphery', since nearly half of retinotopic cortex representing the far periphery (> 11 deg) was not mapped.

3) Results section, paragraph 12, and Figure 7 legend. The legend states that “Average individual subject inter-run correlations between hemispheres......steadily decreased at larger distances for all conditions”, which doesn't match what the figure actually shows. The text has it right: “Indeed, inter-run Fisher-transformed correlations on resting state data showed no effect of radial distance (all ps > 0.05), validating the assumption that noise correlations should not be reliable across runs (Figure 7, blue and black lines).” Please rectify the confusing statement in the legend.

Reviewer #2:

Overall I think this work presents a carefully conducted study. The level of careful evaluation and discussion is very prominent and this work should find an interested readership within the vision neuroscience community.

The authors use a seed-based approach to investigate the spatial distribution of connectivity patterns in rs-FRMI data. Interestingly, this was done using both eyes-closed and 'fixation' resting state fMRI. The paper further suggests that the retinotopic connectivity patterns (during rest as well as movie viewing) are largely organized along iso-eccentricity bands, which might reflect an important feature of cortical visual processing.

The findings are presented along with a number of important checks to rule out some of the more obvious confounds, such as BOLD smearing, eye-movements, subject motion and other nuisances.

The overall bottom-line finding (as e.g. revealed by the authors choice of title and impact statement) of correlation patterns reflecting eccentricity organisation in principle has been demonstrated multiple times before (see e.g. discussion of foveal vs high eccentricity representations in Smith et al 2012 PNAS or Heinzle et al 2011 Neuroimage). Particularly the latter paper already demonstrates that the retinotopic organization of visual cortex can be probed using resting state connectivity fMRI.

Reviewer #3:

This manuscript describes a study into the functional connectivity across several human visual cortical areas derived from conventional fMRI resting-state measurements (under fixation and eyes-closed conditions) and measurements while subjects viewed a movie stimulus. The main finding is that the connectivity exhibits a striking organization across the visual cortical areas in which locations that retinotopically represent the same eccentricity of the visual field tend to be correlated, across adjacent cortical areas as well as across the ventral and dorsal subdivisions and across hemispheres. The consistency of this organization throughout the visual cortical areas argues that it is present both in the presence and absence of bottom-up anatomical connectivity. Steps are taken to control for effects such as receptive field size and spatial spread based on modeling their effects using previously reported measurements.

Overall this manuscript is extremely well written and the results are compelling. Methodologically the approach is well thought out and carefully executed. The intra-run correlation of the movie watching data presented in Figure 7 and the dorsal-ventral correlations in Figure 4B were particularly compelling.

My main concern is in the interpretation of these striking findings. As the authors mention, functional connectivity reflects both direct and indirect anatomical connections, and the authors also mention that there have been no reports of anatomical connectivity that could support the observed correlations across eccentricities. The foveal-peripheral biases that are reviewed could be consistent with these observations. While I acknowledge that this is beyond the scope of the current report to identify the origin of this organizational feature, perhaps the manuscript could address further this issue which may be very challenging to reconcile.

The issue of the effective resolution along the eccentricity coordinate versus the polar angle coordinate was not discussed, and I wonder how this might affect the findings. Because the cortical areas are elongated along the eccentricity direction there are more voxels to sample the progression of eccentricity than there are to sample the progressions of polar angles. Upon examining the plots in Figure 2B (and to some extent the plots in Figure 3B) it appears that there is some consistent correlations across all areas averaged in the retinotopically corresponding region (especially well seen in seeds centered on 1 deg, 2.5 deg, and 5 deg), but also there seems to be some symmetry in the correlation patterns across quadrants in the 2.5 deg and 5 deg maps. One wonders if it is possible that there is a polar angle component to the organization as well, i.e., the correlations may not be only a function of eccentricity but could be a function of polar angle as well. This question gets at my main concern outlined above. Given the reduced resolution in the polar angle direction this question may be difficult to address using this data, and some attempt is made in Figure 8, but if the resolution is not sufficient perhaps the authors could discuss the potential of an unresolved polar angle organization as an alternate possibility.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled “Widespread correlation patterns of fMRI signal across visual cortex reflect eccentricity organization” for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Eve Marder (Senior editor), by Timothy Behrens (BRE), and by the original 3 reviewers.

Often the BRE will choose to handle revisions himself, but on this occasion Tim Behrens wanted to return to the referees as there were some detailed points in the revisions that required their analytical expertise.

We are now almost ready to accept for publication, but there are a few remaining issues about presentation.

The main issue is that one reviewer is still concerned by the absence of any reflection of polar geometry in the data, and by the apparent new claim that this cannot be due to the quality of your data. During the course of the revision, a second paper with higher quality data has shown that it is possible to see reflections of polar geometry in resting connectivity (Gravel et al., http://journal.frontiersin.org/Journal/10.3389/fnins.2014.00339/).

The review panel are not sure why this is difficult to find in your data, but we would like you to be clear in the Introduction and the discussion that such structure is visible in higher quality data. ”

In concert with these changes, we would like you to be slightly clearer about the novelty of your claim with respect to other papers that have shown eccentricity organisation’s – albeit with less detail and precision than you show here.

For example, we do not think that the following statement in the Introduction is a fair reflection of the literature:

“In addition, widespread functional correlation patterns have been observed across visual cortex in both macaques (Leopold et al., 2003; Vincent et al., 2007) and humans (Nir et al., 2006; Nir et al., 2008; Yeo et al., 2011; Donner et al., 2013). The governing principles, if any, of such widespread connectivity patterns are still unknown.”

Reviewer 3 had related concerns that I reproduce here. We do not require you to perform the analysis in point 1 below, if you are clear (as above) that the polar connectivity can be seen in higher quality data, but if you choose to do the analysis, that would be welcome. However, we would like you to address point 2.

When you resubmit your manuscript, it will not go back to review, but will be assessed by BRE member Tim Behrens.

Reviewer #3:

I thank the authors for responding my concerns and for adding the analyses shown in Author response images 3 and 4. The new results presented in Author response image 3, showing that in some cases within and across V2 and V3 (although V1 is not included?) the correlation falls with angular distance, are particularly helpful.

I am not sure, however, that the concern I had raised about the potential asymmetry in the resolving power along the eccentricity coordinate and polar angle coordinate has been completely addressed. First, the analyses are restricted to only eccentricities from 1 degree to about 12 degrees, so it is not clear how much a given fMRI voxel will sample along the eccentricity direction relative to the polar angle direction given the cortical magnification and therefore how marginal the effect would be. Also, the new analysis accounting for the potential statistical biases arising from re-binning the data does not address the fact that there is higher effective spatial resolution of the eccentricity coordinate than the polar angle coordinate. The plots in Author response image 3 are the most direct measure of this, since the observation that in some regions the correlation falls off with distance argues that there may be in some cases enough voxels along the polar angle direction to properly resolve a spatial gradient of correlation. Perhaps the authors could address this issue more directly. (Smoothing the data along the eccentricity direction to yield similar resolution for both directions may be one brute-force approach, but perhaps there is another, better way.)

Still, the new results provided in Author response image 3 highlight that there is some level of “polar angle connectivity”, which was previously only indirectly demonstrated, e.g., in the second and third panels of Figure 2B and in Figure 8. As the authors point out, based on the topographic model regression analyses there is evidence for “local connectivity patterns” including overlapping RF effects and correlations between homotopic regions. Beneath these overlapping RF and homotopic correlations there are also the widespread correlations, and this pattern appears to be weaker in the polar angle direction. Perhaps the authors would consider including the results of Author response image 3 in the main manuscript, and boiling down the results of Figure 9 by reporting the overall variance explained by local connectivity versus widespread connectivity and what proportion of the widespread connectivity is along the eccentricity direction and what proportion is along the polar angle direction. While the authors do point out that these four spatial components are not orthogonal, some clarification of how much of the observed correlations can be explained by widespread patterns would strengthen the manuscript.

results.result: The study demonstrates that BOLD signal correlations in visual cortex reflect both local connectivity based on overlapping receptive fields and widespread connectivity based on eccentricity organization. Strongest correlations were observed between cortical sites with iso-eccentricity representations, even when these sites represented non-overlapping parts of visual space (across upper/lower visual fields and between hemispheres). These patterns were consistent across subjects and experimental conditions.
results.evaluation: The claims are well-supported by extensive seed-based correlation analyses (C20-C27), eccentricity binning analyses (C29-C36), and quantitative statistical tests (C33, C34). The findings are replicated across multiple subjects (C12, C24), different visual areas (C35, C36), and experimental conditions (C25, C27), providing converging evidence for the eccentricity-based correlation pattern.

results.result: Correlation strength decreased linearly as a function of radial distance (eccentricity difference) across all visual area pairs tested. This effect was statistically significant (p < 0.05, FDR-corrected) for nearly all comparisons, with negative slopes ranging from -0.14 to -0.80 across areas. The effect was strongest in early visual areas (V1-V3) and was observed across all experimental conditions.
results.evaluation: The radial distance effect is robustly demonstrated through comprehensive quantitative analyses (C37, C51, C56), statistical testing with permutation controls (C52, C56), and replication across multiple area pairs (C38, C55), conditions (C45, C46, C47), and visual field quadrants (C42-C44). The linear relationship is well-characterized with specific slope values reported.

results.result: Angular distance (polar angle) effects on correlations were observed only for comparisons within visual field quadrants and between mirror-symmetric regions across the vertical meridian, but not between dorsal and ventral regions. This suggests angular connectivity reflects overlapping receptive fields and homotopic connections rather than widespread organization.
results.evaluation: The claims present a clear pattern of positive findings (C57, C58) and negative findings (C60) that together support the interpretation (C59). The selective presence of angular effects only in specific comparisons (within quadrants and mirror-symmetric) provides evidence that angular connectivity is limited to local overlapping RF connections rather than widespread patterns.

results.result: The spatial pattern of eccentricity-based correlations was highly similar across experimental conditions (resting fixation, eyes closed, and movie viewing), with average correlations between conditions of 0.84-0.86 for intra-hemisphere and 0.71-0.75 for inter-hemisphere comparisons. This suggests the pattern reflects an intrinsic functional architecture of the visual system.
results.evaluation: The high quantitative similarity of correlation patterns across conditions (C62, C63) is well-documented and supports the interpretation of intrinsic architecture (C64, C65). The consistency across both resting states and active viewing (C14, C61) provides strong evidence that this organization is stimulus-independent.

results.result: Inter-run correlation analysis during movie viewing showed significant eccentricity-based patterns (96% of comparisons, p < 0.05 FDR-corrected), while resting state inter-run correlations showed no effect of radial distance. This demonstrates that eccentricity-based correlations reflect stimulus processing during naturalistic viewing and are not driven by non-neuronal artifacts.
results.evaluation: The inter-run analysis provides a clever control for artifacts (C66, C67) and demonstrates stimulus-related processing (C68, C69). The contrast between movie and rest conditions (C67 vs C68) and high statistical significance (C69) strongly support the interpretation that these patterns reflect genuine neural processing (C70).

results.result: Extensive control analyses ruled out multiple potential confounds including overlapping RFs, homotopic connections, anatomical distance, BOLD spatial autocorrelation, subject motion, eye movements, and physiological noise. The eccentricity-based correlation pattern could not be explained by any of these factors.
results.evaluation: The claims describe a comprehensive set of control analyses addressing major potential confounds. Each control is supported by specific analyses: artificial data controls (C73), motion correlation analyses (C75-C77), comparison across eye conditions (C78), and inter-run analyses (C79). The convergence of multiple independent controls strongly supports the conclusion (C15, C71).

results.result: Topographic model regression analysis revealed that both local (overlapping RF) and widespread (eccentricity) connectivity patterns contributed to observed correlations. The full model explained 40-68% of variance for intra-areal and 11-28% for inter-areal comparisons. However, collinearity between predictors (mean r=0.54) complicated interpretation of individual predictor contributions.
results.evaluation: The regression analysis is well-executed with clear quantitative results (C84) and appropriate statistical testing (C85-C87). The authors appropriately acknowledge the collinearity issue (C88, C89) and its implications for interpretation. The inference that overlapping RF cannot fully explain widespread effects (C90) is supported by the eccentricity bin analyses showing correlations between non-overlapping regions.

results.result: After removing variance explained by local connectivity (overlapping RF and noise), significant eccentricity effects remained for 56/60 area pairs (p < 0.05, FDR-corrected), while polar angle effects were significant for only 4/60 pairs. Eccentricity residual correlations were significantly stronger than polar angle for 49/60 pairs, demonstrating that widespread connectivity is anisotropic and reflects eccentricity organization.
results.evaluation: The residual correlation analysis effectively addresses the collinearity issue from the full model by removing shared variance. The stark contrast between eccentricity (56/60 significant) and polar angle (4/60 significant) effects (C93, C96, C97) provides strong evidence for the anisotropic nature of widespread connectivity (C101). The conservative approach of attributing shared variance to local connectivity (C99) strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: The variance explained by local connectivity models was equally correlated with eccentricity (mean r=0.50) and polar angle (mean r=0.49) predictors, with minimal difference between them (mean difference=0.01). This suggests that local connectivity based on overlapping RFs is isotropic with respect to visual field, while widespread connectivity beyond overlapping RFs specifically reflects eccentricity organization.
results.evaluation: The quantitative comparison (C102) demonstrates isotropy of local connectivity, which is consistent with anatomical studies cited (C103). This finding, combined with the anisotropic widespread effects, supports the key conclusion that eccentricity organization is a property of widespread, not local, connectivity (C104). The logic is sound and well-supported.

results.result: For inter-hemisphere comparisons, homotopic RF connectivity captured more variance than overlapping RF connectivity. However, after removing all variance explained by homotopic RF connectivity, eccentricity effects remained in residual correlations, demonstrating that eccentricity-based connectivity is not driven by homotopic connections.
results.evaluation: The homotopic connectivity control is appropriate given the known importance of callosal connections. The finding that eccentricity effects persist after removing homotopic variance (C106) provides strong evidence that the widespread pattern is not simply explained by mirror-symmetric connections (C107). The analysis is well-designed and the conclusion is justified.

results.result: Quantitative comparison of model contributions showed that for within-hemisphere comparisons, overlapping RF explained more variance than residual widespread connectivity (ratio 1.69:1.00). For between-hemisphere comparisons, widespread connectivity dominated without accounting for homotopy (ratio 1.00:5.65), but overlapping RF was greater when including homotopic connections (ratio 1.27:1.00). Notably, eccentricity correlations were similar within and across hemispheres after accounting for overlapping RF, suggesting uniform coverage across the visual field.
results.evaluation: The quantitative comparisons (C108, C109) provide clear evidence for the relative contributions of local and widespread connectivity in different contexts. The interpretation that eccentricity patterns uniformly span the visual field (C113) is well-supported by the similarity of residual correlations within and across hemispheres. The conclusions appropriately synthesize the model results (C110, C111, C112).

results.result: The study extends prior fMRI findings by explicitly combining local (overlapping RF) and widespread connectivity analyses across a wider range of visual areas. While previous studies reported fine-scale overlapping RF patterns and coarse foveal-peripheral distinctions, this study demonstrates a systematic, fine-grained eccentricity-based correlation pattern across the entire visual field that persists after controlling for overlapping RFs and cortical distance.
results.evaluation: The claims accurately characterize prior work (C115-C119) and clearly articulate the study's novel contributions (C120, C121). The distinction between previous coarse-scale findings and the current fine-grained systematic pattern (C122) is well-supported by the data. The positioning relative to prior literature is appropriate and well-documented with citations.

results.result: The eccentricity-based correlation patterns observed during rest (without visual input) and during movie viewing (with strong bottom-up input) suggest this organization reflects an intrinsic functional architecture of visual cortex. This is consistent with prior findings in macaques and cats showing that neurons with similar response properties are correlated in presence and absence of external input.
results.evaluation: The interpretation of intrinsic architecture (C123, C127) is well-supported by the consistency of patterns across conditions (C124, C125) and is appropriately contextualized with prior neurophysiological findings (C126). The inference is reasonable given the data, though the exact mechanisms remain to be determined.

results.result: The observed functional connectivity patterns may reflect both direct and indirect anatomical connections. Local connectivity likely reflects direct connections between overlapping RFs, while widespread eccentricity-based patterns may reflect broader anatomical organization with eccentricity-dependent projections between early and higher-order visual areas, potentially mediated by feedback from extrastriate areas with large receptive fields.
results.evaluation: While the discussion of potential anatomical substrates is well-informed by prior literature (C129, C131, C132, C136), the claims are largely speculative (C128, C135, C139). The authors appropriately acknowledge gaps in current anatomical knowledge (C137) and note that the exact relationship needs further investigation (C141). The prediction of gradient organization (C138) is reasonable but untested. The observation about V2/V4 connectivity patterns (C140) is interesting but inferential.

results.result: The findings link early and higher-order visual cortex organization by demonstrating that eccentricity-based functional architecture is evident even in early visual areas. This connects to prior proposals that eccentricity organizes higher-order cortex, with foveal-biased areas specialized for face/object recognition and peripheral-biased areas for scene analysis, reflecting different computational requirements and visual acuity needs.
results.evaluation: The interpretation linking early and higher-order organization (C142, C151) is well-supported by the data and appropriately contextualized with prior literature on higher-order visual cortex (C143, C144, C150) and perceptual requirements (C145-C149). The connection between the current findings and established principles of visual system organization is logical and well-articulated.

results.result: The study demonstrates the importance of relating functional connectivity to known functional organization. The detailed retinotopic organization of visual cortex provided a unique opportunity for systematic comparison. Notably, correlations were stronger between areas at matched eccentricities than within areas at large eccentricity distances, suggesting functional connectivity analyses are more sensitive to widespread inter-areal patterns than to localization of individual areas.
results.evaluation: The methodological insights (C152, C155) are well-supported by the study's approach and findings. The observation about relative sensitivity (C154) is an interesting and important finding with implications for connectivity methodology. The claims appropriately emphasize the value of relating connectivity to known organization (C153) and are supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: The study examined 14 healthy subjects (aged 24-34, 6 females) with normal/corrected vision who were experienced MRI subjects trained to maintain fixation. Retinotopic organization was mapped within central 15° using standard traveling wave paradigms to define visual areas V1, V2, V3, V3A-B, hV4, VO1-2.
results.evaluation: The methodological claims are clearly stated and appropriate. Sample size (n=14) is reasonable for fMRI studies with within-subject designs. Subject selection criteria (C157, C158) and training (C159) are appropriate for minimizing confounds. The retinotopic mapping approach (C18) is standard and well-established.

results.result: Individual node correlation coefficients with all other nodes in visual cortex typically ranged between -0.10 and 0.75 after CSF and white matter signal regression.
results.evaluation: This is a straightforward descriptive statistic from the data analysis (C19). The range is reasonable for resting-state fMRI correlations after standard preprocessing. The claim is well-supported.

results.result: Background claims establish that the human visual system contains over two-dozen retinotopically organized areas, that topographic organization supports information integration, and that prior studies have demonstrated both local connectivity based on overlapping RFs and widespread correlation patterns with foveal-peripheral distinctions.
results.evaluation: These are well-established background claims appropriately supported by citations to primary literature and reviews (C1, C5-C11). The characterization of prior work is accurate and provides appropriate context for the current study.

results.result: The authors propose that the eccentricity-based correlation pattern is part of an intrinsic functional architecture supporting integration of information across functionally specialized visual areas and could reflect eccentricity-dependent processing.
results.evaluation: This interpretive claim (C4, C16) is well-supported by the extensive data showing consistent eccentricity-based patterns across conditions, areas, and subjects. While the exact functional role remains speculative, the characterization as intrinsic architecture is justified by the resting-state findings and consistency across conditions. The proposal is appropriately framed as interpretation rather than definitive conclusion.

results.result: Strong correlations with nodes adjacent to the seed and within ipsilateral dorsal cortex likely reflect well-established connectivity based on overlapping visual field representations, but may also reflect intrinsic spatial spread of the BOLD signal.
results.evaluation: This interpretation (C22) appropriately acknowledges both the likely neural basis (overlapping RFs) supported by prior literature and a potential confound (BOLD spread). The authors appropriately cite relevant studies and acknowledge uncertainty. This measured interpretation is appropriate for seed-based correlation findings.

results.result: Individual subject and group average correlation patterns were similar to previously reported group average patterns from Yeo et al. (2011).
results.evaluation: This comparison to prior literature (C28) provides validation of the general approach and findings. The claim is appropriately supported by citation and suggests the results are consistent with established patterns.

results.result: The stronger correlations with radial distance in early visual areas (V1, V2, V3) could reflect relatively smaller, more spatially focal receptive fields or larger surface area providing more data points.
results.evaluation: This is a speculative interpretation (C40) of an observed pattern (C39). Both proposed explanations are plausible but neither is directly tested. The claim appropriately uses tentative language ("could reflect") but remains uncertain without additional analysis to distinguish between these possibilities.

results.result: Eccentricity-based correlation patterns persisted after removal of horizontal and vertical meridian data, demonstrating effects are unlikely driven by local, overlapping visual field representations.
results.evaluation: This control analysis (C48) effectively addresses a potential confound where meridian representations might drive apparent eccentricity effects through local connectivity. The persistence of effects after meridian removal strengthens the conclusion that widespread patterns are genuine. The analysis is well-designed and the inference is justified.
